analysis.investment_thesis: Century Plyboards fails both Magic Formula tests decisively: Earnings Yield of ~2.6% (EBIT ₹487 Cr / EV ~₹18,499 Cr) is far below the 6% minimum threshold, and ROCE of 10.4% falls well short of the 20%+ required for a quality business. A 9-year net profit CAGR of just 1.0% against a P/E of 69.8x means investors are paying a luxury price for a commodity-grade compounder.
key_strengths: Strong brand portfolio (SAINIK, CENTURYPLY) driving 11.9% revenue CAGR over 9 years
High gross margin of 47.3% suggesting real pricing power at the product level
Promoter holding of 71.8% aligns management with long-term outcomes
key_risks: Debt explosion: borrowings surged from ₹165 Cr (2021) to ₹1,643 Cr (2025) — a 10x jump in 4 years
Free cash flow deeply negative: -₹666 Cr in 2025 and -₹593 Cr in 2024 due to massive capex (₹665–850 Cr/yr)
Operating profit deteriorating: EBITDA fell from ₹621 Cr (2023) to ₹496 Cr (2025) even as revenue grew — margin compression
red_flags: Operating CF turned negative in 2025 (-₹3 Cr) for the first time — a business funding capex entirely via debt
Finance costs quintupled from ₹13 Cr (2021) to ₹69 Cr (2025) and will compound as debt compounds
Net profit CAGR of 1.0% over 9 years — effectively zero real earnings growth adjusted for inflation
EV/EBITDA of 30.9x on declining and suppressed EBITDA — valuation assumes a flawless execution turnaround
analysis.detailed_analysis:
Magic Formula math is brutal here. EBIT in FY2025 was ₹487 Cr against an Enterprise Value of roughly ₹18,499 Cr (market cap ₹16,933 Cr + net debt ~₹1,566 Cr), yielding an Earnings Yield of just 2.6% — less than a quarter of the 12% threshold I consider attractive. Return on Capital (ROCE) is 10.4%, well below the 20%+ I require to call a business genuinely high-quality. The story gets worse in combination: this is a capital-hungry, margin-thin manufacturer trading as if it were a premium consumer franchise.

The capex cycle is the central issue. Between FY2022 and FY2025, Century Plyboards burned ₹2,289 Cr in capex and ₹1,304 Cr in cumulative negative FCF while borrowings ballooned 7x. The thesis — that MDF/particle board capacity will unlock a new earnings base — may eventually play out, but the numbers today show EBITDA declining (₹621 Cr in 2023 → ₹496 Cr in 2025) even as revenues grow, meaning the new capacity is not yet contributing and interest costs are already biting. At 69.8x trailing P/E, the market is pricing in a near-perfect recovery. The Magic Formula demands both cheapness and quality; this stock offers neither right now.
